body:
Carlyle Buys Chungho Nais, While TPG Acquires Lotte Rental for 1.3 Trillion Won Top Two Car Rental Firms Both Now in Private Equity Hands "Little Exposure to Economic Shocks, Steady Cash Inflows" "Bright Market Outlook Makes Exits Smoother"

Private equity firms are racing to buy up South Korea's rental businesses, with deep-pocketed foreign managers leading the charge for market share. Analysts say the business model — which collects subscription fees every month — matches what private equity managers prize most: predictable cash flow. The potential to expand the business using customer data is another reason the sector looks attractive to buyout funds.

Texas Pacific Group (TPG) will close its acquisition of Lotte Rental as early as this month, according to investment banking sources on the 4th. The deal covers a 61.2% controlling stake, valued at a total of 1.31 trillion won ($920 million). In June, Carlyle bought Chungho Nais from the bereaved family of its founder for 1 trillion won. Before that, Affinity Equity Partners acquired a 100% stake in SK Rent-a-Car for 820 billion won in August 2024. Among domestic firms, MBK Partners bought and operated Woongjin Coway starting in 2013. Game developer Netmarble is now Coway's largest shareholder.

Korea's rental market splits broadly into two categories: home appliances such as water purifiers and bidets, and vehicles. Chungho Nais operates mainly in the appliance segment, where five companies together hold about 80% of the market. Chungho Nais is estimated to hold roughly 10%. Its revenue rose about 7% from a year earlier to 510.2 billion won last year, though operating profit fell to 44.9 billion won from 65 billion won as competition intensified. In car rentals, Lotte Rental and SK Rent-a-Car rank first and second, with a combined 40% share. The Fair Trade Commission earlier this year blocked Affinity Equity Partners, the owner of SK Rent-a-Car, from acquiring Lotte Rental. Lotte Rental posted revenue of 2.92 trillion won last year, ahead of SK Rent-a-Car's 1.56 trillion won.

Private equity managers must distribute returns to limited partners on a regular schedule under their fund agreements, making stable cash flow a priority. Unlike one-time product sales, rental contracts bring in subscription fees every month, giving managers steady and predictable inflows. The customer data also lets operators recommend additional rental products or expand into care services. Chungho Nais runs a vertically integrated subscription platform spanning finished-product rentals, core component manufacturing, installation and maintenance. Car rental operators can collect rental fees during the contract term and then earn additional income by selling the vehicles on the used-car market.

"Businesses with limited exposure to economic cycles and predictable income over the contract term are favored by private equity managers," an investment banking official said. "The vertically integrated structure is another attractive point, because it allows maximum efficiency with a small workforce." A bright market outlook is another draw, since the ultimate aim of any buyout is to sell the company later at a higher price. Meritz Securities projects that Korea's home appliance rental market will grow to 11.8 trillion won by 2030 from 5.4 trillion won in 2020, driven by factors including the rise in single-person households. The car rental market is expected to top 10 trillion won for the first time this year and reach 13 trillion won by 2030.
